title: Virtuosos
objective: After this level you can explain how Paganini and Liszt became superstars.
summary: Paganini's playing sparked devil rumors; Liszt brought his effects to the piano, gave the first solo recitals (London, 1840) and inspired Lisztomania.

cards.headline: People whispered that his violin playing came from the devil.
cards.body: Niccolò Paganini played so impossibly well that stories spread he was in league with the devil, and even that he'd been in prison for murder. Rumors, not facts. But they show how unreal his playing seemed, and how much attention one performer could command.

cards.headline: Paganini: the violin, pushed to extremes
cards.body: Born in Genoa in 1782, Paganini wrote 24 Caprices for solo violin, packed with the tricks that made his name: glassy harmonics and plucked pizzicato. His tours made him famous across Europe, and his appearances in Paris and London in 1831 were sensations. He wrote them to show off one player, and they still do.

cards.headline: Liszt: the Paganini of the piano
cards.body: The Hungarian-born pianist Franz Liszt heard Paganini play and resolved to carry his violin effects over to the piano. He went further: he gave the first complete solo piano recitals. In London in 1840 he billed his concerts as 'Liszt's Pianoforte Recitals', the first time 'recital' was used for music. Until then, the word meant a dramatic reading.

cards.headline: Lisztomania
cards.body: Audiences lost their heads. Drawings of the time show women swooning and flowers flying at the stage. In 1844 the poet Heinrich Heine gave the craze a name: Lisztomania. His friend Chopin, meanwhile, preferred intimate settings to big halls. Same city, same instrument, opposite ideas of what a concert should be.

mascot.line: Long before stadium tours, there was one man and one piano. And flowers. So many flowers.
